59550:22:# scDblFinder
59551-23-
59552:24:The `scDblFinder` method combines the strengths of various doublet detection approaches, 
59553-25-training an iterative classifier on the neighborhood of real cells and artificial doublets.
59554-26-
59555:27:`scDblFinder()` has two main modes of operation: cluster-based or not.
59556-28-Both perform quite well (see [Germain et al., 2021](https://f1000research.com/articles/10-979)).
59557-29-In general, we recommend the cluster-based approach in datasets with a very clear cluster structure, and the random approach in more complex datasets.

59606-78-The `clusters` argument can be either a vector of cluster labels for each column of `sce`, a colData column of `sce` containing such labels, or `TRUE`.
59607-79-If `clusters=TRUE`, the fast clustering approach (see `?fastcluster`) will be employed.
59608-80-If normalized expression (assay 'logcounts') and/or PCA (reducedDim 'PCA') are already present in the object, these will be used for the clustering step.
59609-81-
59610-82-### Multiple samples
59611-83-
59612-84-If you have multiple samples (understood as different cell captures), then it is
59613-85-preferable to look for doublets separately for each sample (for multiplexed samples with cell hashes, 
59614-86-this means for each batch). You can do this by simply providing a vector of the sample ids to the 
59615:87:`samples` parameter of `scDblFinder` or, if these are stored in a column of `colData`, the name of the 
59616-88-column. In this case, you might also consider multithreading it using the `BPPARAM` parameter (assuming you've got enough RAM!). 
59617-89-For example:
59618-90-
59619-91-```{r, eval=FALSE}
59620-92-library(BiocParallel)
59621:93:sce <- scDblFinder(sce, samples="sample_id", BPPARAM=MulticoreParam(3))
59622:94:table(sce$scDblFinder.class)
59623-95-```
59624-96-
59625-97-Note that if you are running multiple samples using the cluster-based approach (see below), clustering will be performed sample-wise.
59626:98:While this is typically not an issue for doublet identification, it means that the cluster labels (and putative origins of doublets) won't match between samples. If you are interested in these, it is preferable to first cluster (for example using `sce$cluster <- fastcluster(sce)`) and then provide the clusters to `scDblFinder`, which will ensure concordant labels across samples.
59627-99-
59628-100-Of note, if you have very large differences in number of cells between samples the scores will not be directly comparable. We are working on improving this, but in the meantime it would be preferable to stratify similar samples and threshold the sets separately.
59629-101-
59630-102-<br/><br/>
59631-103-
59632-104-## Description of the method
59633-105-
59634:106:Wrapped in the `scDblFinder` function are the following steps:
59635-107-
59636-108-### Splitting captures
59637-109-
59638:110:Doublets can only arise within a given sample or capture, and for this reason are better sought independently for each sample, which also speeds up the analysis. If the `samples` argument is given, `scDblFinder` will use it to split the cells into samples/captures, and process each of them in parallel if the `BPPARAM` argument is given. Depending on the `multiSampleMode` argument, the classifier can be trained globally, with thresholds optimized on a per-sample basis; however we did not see an improvement in doing so, and therefore by default each sample is treated separately to maximize robustness to technical differences.
59639-111-
59640-112-If your samples are multiplexed, i.e. the different samples are mixed in different batches, then the batches should be what you provide to this argument.
59641-113-
59642-114-### Reducing and clustering the data
59643-115-
59644-116-The analysis can be considerably sped up, at little if any cost in accuracy, by reducing the dataset to only the top expressed genes (controlled by the `nfeatures` argument).
59645-117-
59646-118-Then, depending on the `clusters` argument, an eventual PCA and clustering (using the internal `fastcluster` function) will be performed.
59647---
59648-120-An alternative approach, however, is to generate doublets randomly (setting `clusters` to FALSE or NULL), and use the iterative approach (see below) to exclude also unidentifiable artificial doublets from the training.
59649-121-
59650-122-### Generating artificial doublets
59651-123-
59652-124-Depending on the `clusters` and `propRandom` arguments, artificial doublets will be generated by combining random cells and/or pairs of non-identical clusters (this can be performed manually using the `getArtificialDoublets` function). A proportion of the doublets will simply use the sum of counts of the composing cells, while the rest will undergo a library size adjustment and poisson resampling.
59653-125-
59654-126-### Examining the k-nearest neighbors (kNN) of each cell
59655-127-
59656:128:A new PCA is performed on the combination of real and artificial cells, from which a kNN network is generated. Using this kNN, a number of parameters are gathered for each cell, such as the proportion of doublets (i.e. artificial doublets or known doublets provided through the `knownDoublets` argument, if given) among the KNN, ratio of the distances to the nearest doublet and nearest non-doublet, etc. Several of this features are reported in the output with the 'scDblFinder.' prefix, e.g.:
59657-129-
59658-130-* `distanceToNearest` : distance to the nearest cell (real or artificial)
59659-131-* `ratio` : the proportion of the KNN that are doublets. (If more than one value of `k` is given, the various ratios will be used during classification and will be reported)
59660-132-* `weighted` : the proportion of the KNN that are doublets, weighted by their distance (useful for isolated cells)
59661-133-
59662-134-### Training a classifier
59663-135-
59664:136:Unless the `score` argument is set to 'weighted' or 'ratio' (in which case the aforementioned ratio is directly used as a doublet score), `scDblFinder` then uses gradient boosted trees trained on the kNN-derived properties along with a few additional features (e.g. library size, number of non-zero features, and an estimate of the difficultly of detecting artificial doublets in the cell's neighborhood, a variant of the `cxds` score from the `r Biocpkg("scds","scds")`, etc.) to distinguish doublets (either artificial or given) from other cells, and assigns a score on this basis. 
59665-137-
59666-138-One problem of using a classifier for this task is that some of the real cells (the actual doublets) are mislabeled as singlet, so to speak. 
59667:139:`scDblFinder` therefore iteratively retrains the classifier, each time excluding from the training the (real) cells called as doublets in the previous step (as well as unidentifiable artificial doublets). The number of steps being controlled by the `iter` parameter (in our experience, 2 or 3 is optimal).
59668-140-
59669:141:This score is available in the output, in the `scDblFinder.score` colData column, and can be interpreted as a probability. If the data is multi-sample, a single model is trained for all samples.
59670-142-
59671-143-### Thresholding
59672-144-
59673:145:Rather than thresholding on some arbitrary cutoff of the score, `scDblFinder` uses the expected number of doublets in combination to the misclassification rate to establish a threshold. Unless it is manually given through the `dbr` argument, the expected doublet rate is first estimated (see below). If samples were specified, and if the `dbr` is automatically calculated, thresholding is performed separately across samples.
59674-146-
59675-147-Thresholding then tries to simultaneously minimize: 1) the classification error (in terms of the proportion of known doublets below the threshold) and 2) the deviation from the expected number of doublets among real cells (as a ratio of the total number of expected doublets within the range determined by `dbr.sd`, and adjusted for homotypic doublets). This means that, if you have no idea about the doublet rate, setting `dbr.sd=1` will make the threshold depend entirely on the misclassification rate.
59676-148-
59677-149-### Doublet origins and enrichments
59678-150-
59679-151-If artificial doublets are generated between clusters, it is sometimes possible to call the most likely origin (in terms of the combination of clusters) of a given putative real doublet.
59680-152-We observed that at least one of the two composing cell is typically recognized, but that both are seldom correctly recognized, owing to the sometimes small relative contribution of one of the two original cells.
59681:153:This information is provided through the `scDblFinder.mostLikelyOrigin` column of the output (and the `scDblFinder.originAmbiguous` column indicates whether this origin is ambiguous or rather clear).
59682-154-This, in turn, allows us to identify enrichment over expectation for specific kinds of doublets.
59683:155:Some statistics on each combination of clusters are saved in `metadata(sce)$scDblFinder.stats`, and the `plotDoubletMap` function can be used to visualize enrichments.
59684-156-In addition, two frameworks are offered for testing the significance of enrichments:
59685-157-
59686-158-* The `clusterStickiness` function tests whether each cluster forms more doublet than would be expected given its abundance, by default using a single quasi-binomial model fitted across all doublet types.
59687-159-* The `doubletPairwiseEnrichment` function separately tests whether each specific doublet type (i.e. combination of clusters) is more abundant than expected, by default using a poisson model.
59688-160-
59689-161-<br/><br/>
59690-162-
59691-163-## Some important parameters
59692-164-
59693:165:`scDblFinder` has a fair number of parameters governing the preprocessing, generation of doublets, classification, etc. (see `?scDblFinder`). Here we describe just a few of the most important ones.
59694-166-
59695-167-### Expected proportion of doublets
59696-168-
59697-169-The expected proportion of doublets has no impact on the density of artificial doublets in the neighborhood, but impacts the classifier's score and, especially, where the cutoff will be placed. It is specified through the `dbr` parameter, as well as `dbr.per1k` (which specifies, if `dbr` is omitted, the rate per thousands cells from which to estimate it). In addition, the `dbr.sd` parameter specifies a +/- range around `dbr` within which the deviation from `dbr` will be considered null.
59698-170-
59699-171-For most platforms, the more cells you capture the higher the chance of creating a doublet.
59700-172-For standard 10X data, the 10X documentation indicates a doublet rate of roughly 0.8\% per 1000 cells captured, which is the default value of `dbr.per1k`. This means that unless `dbr` is manually set, with 5000 cells, (0.008\*5)\*5000 = 200 doublets are expected, and the default expected doublet rate will be set to this value (with a default standard deviation of 0.015). Note however that different protocols may vary in the expected proportion of doublets. For example, the high-throughput (HT) 10X kit has an expected doublet rate of half the standard, i.e. 0.4\% per 1000 cells, so if using that kit, set `dbr.per1k=0.004`.
59701-173-
59702-174-Also note that strictly speaking, the proportion of doublets depends more on the number of cells inputted than that recovered. If your recovery rate was lower than expected, you might observe a higher doublet rate (see the [too-many doublets](#toomany) section below).
59703-175-
59704-176-The impact of the expected doublet rate on the thresholding will depend on how hard the classification task is: if it is easy, the called doublets will not depend much on the expected rate. **If you are unsure about the doublet rate, you might consider increasing `dbr.sd`**: with a high value (e.g. 1), the thresholding will be entirely based on the misclassification error (without any assumption about an expected doublet rate).
59705-177-
59706-178-### Number of artificial doublets
59707-179-
59708:180:The number of artificial doublets can be set through the `artificialDoublets` parameter. Using more artificial doublets leads to a better sampling of the possible mixtures of cells, but increases memory and runtime, and can skew the scores, in extreme cases leading to difficulties in setting a threshold for being called as a doublet (see [this issue](https://github.com/plger/scDblFinder/issues/79) for a discussion).
59709-181-
59710:182:By default, `scDblFinder` will generate roughly as many artificial doublets as there are cells, which is usually appropriate. However, for very small datasets this could represent an undersampling of the mixing space and hence lead to lower detection accuracy. For this reason, a hard minimum number of artificial doublet is set. This will tend to improve accuracy for small datasets, but the scores will be skewed towards 1, possibly making a separation difficult. If you are in such a situation and your histogram of scores does not show a bimodality, consider manually setting the `artificialDoublets` parameter to something closer to your actual number of cells.
59711-183-
59712-184-<br/><br/>
59713-185-
59714-186-## Frequently-asked questions
59715-187-
59716-188-### I'm getting way too many doublets called - what's going on? {#toomany}
59717-189-
59718-190-Then you most likely have a wrong doublet rate. If you did not provide it (`dbr` argument), the doublet rate will be calculated automatically using expected doublet rates from 10x, meaning that the more cells captured, the higher the doublet rates. If you have reasons to think that this is not applicable to your data, set the `dbr` manually.
59719-191-
59720:192:The most common cause for an unexpectedly large proportion of doublets is if you have a multi-sample dataset and did not split by samples. `scDblFinder` will think that the data is a single capture with loads of cells, and hence with a very high doublet rate. Splitting by sample should solve the issue.
59721-193-
59722:194:Also note that, although 10X-like data tends to have roughly 1\% per 1000 cells captured, the determining factor for doublet formation is the number of cells inserted into the machine. If for some reason your recovery rate is lower than expected, you might have a higher doublet rate than you'd expect from the captured and called cells (in other words, it would be preferable to say that the doublet rate is roughly 0.6\% per 1000 cells put into the machine, where 0.6 is the recovery rate). In such circumstances, `scDblFinder` typically sets the thresholds correctly nevertheless. This is because the thresholding tries to minimize both the deviation from the expected number of doublets and the misclassification (i.e. of artificial doublets), meaning that the effective (i.e. final) doublet rate will differ from the given one. `scDblFinder` also considers false positives to be less problematic than false negatives. You can reduce to some degree the deviation from the input doublet rate by setting `dbr.sd=0`.
59723-195-
59724-196-Finally, note that version (1.20.0) initially shipped with the current Bioconductor release (3.20) version included a wrong default doublet rate (`dbr.per1k`) argument (it was 0.08 instead of 0.008). This was subsequently fixed in version 1.20.2, but if you installed before that you might need to update the package.
59725-197-
59726-198-### Should I use the cluster-based doublet generation or not?
59727-199-
59728:200:Both approaches perform very similarly overall in benchmarks (see the [scDblFinder paper](https://f1000research.com/articles/10-979/)).
59729-201-If your data is very clearly segregated into clusters, or if you are interested in the origin of the doublets, the cluster-based approach is preferable. This will also enable a more accurate accounting of homotypic doublets, and therefore a slightly better thresholding.
59730-202-Otherwise, and especially if your data does not segregate very clearly into clusters, the random approach (e.g. `clusters=FALSE`, the default) is preferable.
59731-203-
59732-204-### The clusters don't make any sense!
59733-205-
59734:206:If you ran `scDblFinder` on a multi-sample dataset and did not provide the cluster labels, then the labels are sample-specific (meaning that label '1' in one sample might have nothing to do with label '1' in another), and plotting them on a tSNE will look like they do not make sense. For this reason, when running multiple samples we recommend to first cluster all samples together (for example using `sce$cluster <- fastcluster(sce)`) and then provide the clusters to `scDblFinder`.
59735-207-
59736-208-### 'Size factors should be positive' error
59737-209-
59738-210-You will get this error if you have some cells that have zero reads (or a very low read count, leading to zero after feature selection). After filtering out these cells the error should go away.
59739-211-
59740-212-### Identifying homotypic doublets
59741-213-
59742:214:Like other similar tools, scDblFinder focuses on identifying heterotypic doublets (formed by different cell types), and has only a low performance in identifying homotypic doublets (see [this preprint](https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.08.04.552078)). This can lead to disagreements with doublets called using cell hashes or SNPs in multiplexed samples, which capture both types of doublets similarly (and can miss intra-sample heterotypic doublets, especially if the multiplexing is low). This is why we treat these approaches as complementary.
59743-215-
59744:216:However, should you for some reason try to identify also homotypic doublets with scDblFinder, be sure to not to use the cluster-based approach, and to set `removeUnidentifiable=FALSE`. Otherwise, scDblFinder removes artificial doublets likely to be homotypic from training, therefore focusing the task on heterotypic doublets, but at the expense ot homotypic ones (which are typically deemed relatively harmless).
59745-217-
59746-218-### What is a sample exactly? Usage with barcoded and 10X Flex data.
59747-219-
59748-220-As indicated above, the `samples` argument should be used to indicate different captures.
59749-221-For multiplexed samples, this is expected to be the batch of cells processed together, rather than the actual samples.
59750-222-
59751-223-In highly multiplexed datasets such as produced by the 10X Flex kit (especially 16-plex), this can cause two kinds of problems.
59752-224-First, the whole logic of the Flex approach is that inter-sample doublets can be resolved into separate cells, and while a large number of unresolvable intra-sample doublets will remain (see [Howitt et al., 2024](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.03.616596v2)), the expected remaining doublet rate will not be the same as for classical 10X experiment. For this reason, we recommend to set a higher `dbr.sd` in such circumstances, e.g. `dbr.sd=1` to base the thresholding entirely on the classification accuracy.
59753-225-
59754:226:Another, more practical problem is that, with such kits, the very large number of cells in a single capture might translante into very large computational demands when running `scDblFinder`. To circumvent such problem, one can split a batch of cells into more decently-sized chunks and process the chunks separately, so long as each chunk is representative of the whole batch in terms of cell heterogeneity.
59755-227-
59756-228-### How can I make this reproducible?
59757-229-
59758:230:Because it relies on the partly random generation of artificial doublets, running scDblFinder multiple times on the same data will yield slightly different results.
59759-231-You can ensure reproducibility using `set.seed()`, however this will not be sufficient when processing multiple samples (i.e. using the `samples` argument -- even without multithreading!).
59760-232-In such case, the seed needs to be passed to the BPPARAMs:
59761-233-
59762-234-```
59763-235-bp <- MulticoreParam(3, RNGseed=1234)
59764:236:sce <- scDblFinder(sce, clusters="cluster", samples="sample", BPPARAM=bp)
59765-237-```
59766-238-
59767-239-Similarly, when processing the samples serially, use `SerialParam(RNGseed = seed)`.
59768-240-
59769:241:(Note that in `BiocParallel` versions <1.28, one had in addition to explicitly start the cluster before the run using `bpstart(bp)`, and then `bpstop(bp)` after `scDblFinder`.)
59770-242-
59771:243:As a final note: when running `scDblFinder` twice on the same data with different random seeds, the scores will be highly correlated, but some cells will be called as doublets (with a high score) in only one of the runs (e.g. see [this issue](https://github.com/plger/scDblFinder/issues/106)). There are good reasons to believe that these are `homotypic doublets` (if doublets at all), and if you worry chiefly about hetertypic doublets, you may concentrate on those that are reprocibly called across runs.
59772-244-
59773-245-### Can I use this in combination with Seurat or other tools?
59774-246-
59775:247:If the input SCE already contains a `logcounts` assay or a `reducedDim` slot named 'PCA', scDblFinder will use them for the clustering step. In addition, a clustering can be manually given using the `clusters` argument of `scDblFinder()`. In this way, `r Githubpkg("satijalab.org/seurat")` clustering could for instance be used to create the artificial doublets (see `?Seurat::as.SingleCellExperiment.Seurat` for conversion to SCE).
59776-248-For example, assuming as `Seurat` object `se`, the following could be done:
59777-249-

59781:253:se$scDblFinder.score <- sce$scDblFinder.score
59782-254-```
59783-255-

59785:257:If you wish this step to be performed differently, you may provide your own function for doing so (see the ``processing`` argument in `?scDblFinder`). We note, however, that the impact of variations of this step on doublet detection is rather mild.
59786-258-In fact, not performing any normalization at all for instance decreases doublet identification accuracy, but by rather little.

59835-307-
59836-308-### Can this be used with scATACseq data?
59837-309-
59838-310-Yes, see the [scATAC vignette](scATAC.html) specifically on this topic.
59839-311-
59840-312-### Should I run QC cell filtering before or after doublet detection?
59841-313-
59842:314:The input to `scDblFinder` should not include empty droplets, and it might be necessary to remove cells with a very low coverage (e.g. <200 or 500 reads) to avoid errors.
59843-315-Further quality filtering should be performed _downstream_ of doublet detection, for two reasons:
59844:316:1. the default expected doublet rate is calculated on the basis of the cells given, and if you excluded a lot of cells as low quality, `scDblFinder` might think that the doublet rate should be lower than it is.
59845-317-2. kicking out all low quality cells first might hamper our ability to detect doublets that are formed by the combination of a good quality cell with a low-quality one.
59846-318-This being said, these are mostly theoretical grounds, and unless your QC filtering is very stringent (and it shouldn't be!), it's unlikely to make a big difference.
59847-319-
59848-320-#### What about ambiant RNA decontamination?
59849-321-
59850-322-Contamination by ambiant RNA has emerged as an important confounder in single-cell (and especially single-nuclei) RNAseq data, which prompts the question of whether that should be run prior or after doublet detection. 
59851-323-Unfortunately, we do not currently have good evidence pointing in either direction, and arguments can be made for both.
59852-324-Low-quality doublets, or doublets from an experiment with a large dominant celltype, can easily look like contamination, and likewise a high amount of contamination can easily look like a doublet because it includes RNA from other cell types.
59853-325-There is a possibility that a decontamination package sees an actual doublet as contamination, and attempts to clean it, which it will necessarily do imperfectly (because while the decontamination is a mixture of all cells, a doublet isn't), but perhaps sufficiently so that it can't be accurately detected as a doublet anymore. This would therefore be an argument for running doublet calling first. 
59854-326-However, it's also possible that decontamination, because it makes the cells cleaner, makes the doublet detection task easier.
59855-327-
59856-328-### Can I combine this method with others?
59857-329-
59858-330-Of course it is always possible to run multiple methods and combine the results.
59859:331:In our benchmark, the combination of scDblFinder with DoubletFinder, for instance, did yield an improvement in most (though not all) datasets (see [the results here](https://github.com/plger/scDblFinder/issues/67#issuecomment-1353590091)), although of a small magnitude.
59860-332-The simplest way is to do an average of the scores (assuming that the scores are on a similar scale, and that a higher score has the same interpretation across methods), which for instance gave similar results to using a Fisher p-value combination on 1-score (interpreted as a probability).

59920-2-title: "Doublet identifiation in single-cell ATAC-seq"
59921-3-author:
59922-4-- name: Pierre-Luc Germain
59923-5-  affiliation: University and ETH Zürich
59924:6:package: scDblFinder

59928-10-  An introduction to the methods implemented for doublet detection in single-cell

59934-21-
59935-22-# Introduction
59936-23-
59937-24-Analyses in single-cell RNAseq are typically limited to a relatively small (e.g. one or two thousands) set of features that are most informative; these are often the genes with a higher expression (and hence more chances of being quantified).
59938-25-In contrast, single-cell ATACseq (scATACseq) data is considerably more sparse, with most reads being spread across hundreds of thousands of regions.
59939-26-In this context, selecting a subset of genes is highly ineffective, and therefore many of the methods developed for single-cell RNAseq are not easily applicable, and need to be adapted.
59940-27-Methods have therefore been developed specifically for scATACseq data (Granja et al. 2021; Thibodeau et al. 2021).
59941-28-
59942:29:This vignette presents different approaches to doublet detection in single-cell ATAC-seq implemented in the package: the first is an adaptation of `scDblFinder`, the second a reimplementation of the AMULET method from Thibodeau et al. (2021). The latter has the advantage of capturing homotypic doublets, but does not perform well in all datasets, and especially requires the cells to have a high library size. We therefore next present two ways of combining the two.
59943-30-
59944:31:# Applying the scDblFinder method
59945-32-
59946:33:With default parameters, the `scDblFinder` method performs very poorly on scATACseq data due to the increase spread of the reads across many features. Since working with all features (i.e. tiles or peaks) is computationally very expensive, an alternative approach is to begin by reducing the size of the dataset, not through _selection_ (as in scRNAseq), but by _aggregating_ correlated features into a relatively small set.
59947-34-This has the advantage of using all information, as well as making the count data more continuous.
59948-35-This method yields comparable performance to specialized single-cell ATACseq software (Germain et al., 2021).
59949-36-
59950-37-The feature aggregation can be triggered using the `aggregateFeatures=TRUE` argument, which will aggregate peak or tile counts into the number of meta-features defined by the `nfeatures`.
59951-38-If the number of meta-features is low (which we recommend), the meta-features can be directly used to calculated distances rather than going through the SVD step (which can be triggered with the `processing` argument). Such an example would be:
59952-39-
59953-40-```{r}
59954:41:suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(scDblFinder))
59955-42-# we use a dummy SingleCellExperiment as example:
59956-43-sce <- mockDoubletSCE(ngenes=300)
59957-44-# setting low number of artificial doublets (same as ncells) just for speedup:
59958:45:sce <- scDblFinder(sce, artificialDoublets=1, aggregateFeatures=TRUE, nfeatures=25, processing="normFeatures")
59959-46-```
59960-47-
59961-48-If you encounter problems running the aggregation-based approach on large datasets, first make sure you have the `mbkmeans` package installed.
59962-49-
59963-50-# Using the Amulet method
59964-51-
59965:52:The AMULET method from Thibodeau et al. (2021) is based on the assumption that, in a diploid cell, any given genomic region should be captured at most twice. Therefore, cells with loci covered by more than two fragments are indicative of the droplet being a doublet. Of note, this approach has the advantage of capturing homotypic doublets, which instead tend to be missed by other methods. Since it was only available in the form of a mixture of java and python scripts, we re-implemented the method in `scDblFinder` (see `?amulet`), leading to equal or superior results to the original implementation (Germain et al. 2021).
59966-53-
59967-54-As in the original implementation, we recommend excluding the mitochondrial and sex chromosomes, as well as repetitive regions. This can be specified with the `regionsToExclude` argument (see the underlying `?getFragmentOverlaps`). It can be used as follows:
59968-55-
59969-56-```{r}
59970-57-# here we use a dummy fragment file for example:

59972-59-
59973-60-# we might also give a GRanges of repeat elements, so that these regions are excluded:
59974-61-suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(GenomicRanges))
59975-62-repeats <- GRanges("chr6", IRanges(1000,2000))
59976-63-# it's better to combine these with mitochondrial and sex chromosomes
59977-64-otherChroms <- GRanges(c("M","chrM","MT","X","Y","chrX","chrY"),IRanges(1L,width=10^8))
59978-65-# here since I don't know what chromosome notation you'll be using I've just put them all,
59979-66-# although this will trigger a warning when combining them:
59980-67-toExclude <- suppressWarnings(c(repeats, otherChroms))
59981-68-# we then launch the method
59982-69-res <- amulet(fragfile, regionsToExclude=toExclude)
59983-70-res
59984-71-```
59985-72-
59986:73:The results is a data.frame with statistics for each barcode, including a p-value. In contrast to the `scDblFinder` score, a lower p-value here is indicative of the droplet being more likely to be a doublet (as in the original method).
59987-74-By default, only the barcodes with a minimum number of reads are considered, but it is possible to specify the droplets for which to gather statistics using the `barcodes` argument.
59988-75-
59989-76-While the package includes an implementation that works based on peak/tile count matrices (see `?amuletFromCounts`), it has a much lower performance with respect to the one based directly on the fragment files (see `?amulet`), and we therefore discourage its use.
59990-77-
59991-78-The workhorse behind the `amulet` function is the `getFragmentOverlaps`, which also includes all of the relevant arguments.
59992-79-If the fragment files are not Tabix-indexed, the whole fragment file will have to be loaded in memory for processing; while this ensures relatively rapid computation, it has high memory requirements. Therefore, if the fragment file is Tabix-indexed (as is for instance done as part of the ArchR pipeline), it will be read and processed per chromosome, which is a little slower due to overhead, but keeps memory requirements rather low. This behavior can be disabled by specifying `fullInMemory=TRUE`.
59993-80-
59994-81-# Combining mehtods
59995-82-
59996:83:While the `scDblFinder`-based approach generally performs well, none of the two approach is optimal across all datasets tested. We therefore investigated two strategies for combining the rationales of each approach.
59997-84-
59998:85:The Amulet method tends to perform best with datasets that have homotypic doublets and where cells have a high library size (i.e. median library size per cell of 10-15k reads), while the `scDblFinder`-based approach works better for heterotypic doublets. Until an optimal solution is found, we recommend using multiple approaches to inform decisions, in particular using the p-value combination method below.
59999-86-
60000-87-## The Clamulet method
60001-88-
60002:89:The `clamulet` method (Classification-powered Amulet-like method) operates similarly to the `scDblFinder` method, but generates artificial doublets by operating on the fragment coverages. This has the advantage that the number of loci covered by more than two reads can be computed for artificial doublets, enabling the use of this feature (along with the kNN-based ones) in a classification scheme. It however has the disadvantage of being rather slow and memory hungry, and appears to be outperformed by a simple p-value combination of the two methods (see below). We therefore _do not_ recommend its usage.
60003-90-
60004:91:The `clamulet` method uses the aforementioned aggregation approach, and its usage includes a number of arguments from both the `scDblFinder` and `amulet` method (see in particular `?getFragmentOverlaps`):

60017-104-

60127-23-
60128-24-# Introduction
60129-25-
60130:26:The `scDblFinder` package gathers various methods for the detection and handling of doublets/multiplets in single-cell sequencing data (i.e. multiple cells captured within the same droplet or reaction volume).
60131-27-This vignette provides a brief overview of the different approaches (which are each covered in their own vignettes) for single-cell RNA sequencing. 
60132-28-*For doublet detection in genomic data, see the [scATACseq vignette](scATAC.html)*. 
60133-29-For a more general introduction to the topic of doublets, refer to the [OCSA book](https://osca.bioconductor.org/doublet-detection.html).
60134-30-
60135-31-All methods require as an input either a matrix of counts or a `r Biocpkg("SingleCellExperiment")` containing count data. With the exception of [findDoubletClusters](findDoubletClusters.html), which operates at the level of clusters (and consequently requires clustering information), all methods try to assign each cell a score indicating its likelihood (broadly understood) of being a doublet.
60136-32-
60137-33-The approaches described here are _complementary_ to doublets identified via cell hashes and SNPs in multiplexed samples: while hashing/genotypes can identify doublets formed by cells of the same type (homotypic doublets) from two samples, which are often nearly undistinguishable from real cells transcriptionally (and hence generally unidentifiable through the present package), it cannot identify doublets made by cells of the same sample, even if they are heterotypic (formed by different cell types). Indeed, recent evidence suggests that doublets are for instance a serious and strongly underestimated issue in 10x Flex datasets (see [Howitt et al., 2024](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.03.616596v2)). Instead, the methods presented here are primarily geared towards the identification of heterotypic doublets, which for most purposes are also the most critical ones.
60138-34-
60139---
60140-37-## computeDoubletDensity
60141-38-
60142-39-The `computeDoubletDensity` method (formerly `scran::doubletCells`) generates random artificial doublets from the real cells, and tries to identify cells whose neighborhood has a high local density of articial doublets. See [computeDoubletDensity](computeDoubletDensity.html) for more information.
60143-40-
60144-41-## recoverDoublets
60145-42-
60146-43-The `recoverDoublets` method is meant to be used when some doublets are already known, for instance through genotype-based calls or cell hashing in multiplexed experiments. The function then tries to identify intra-sample doublets that are neighbors to the known inter-sample doublets. See [recoverDoublets](recoverDoublets.html) for more information.
60147-44-
60148:45:## scDblFinder
60149-46-
60150:47:The `scDblFinder` method combines both known doublets (if available) and cluster-based artificial doublets to identify doublets. The approach builds and improves on a variety of earlier efforts, and is at present the most accurate approach included in this package. See [scDblFinder](scDblFinder.html) for more information.
60151-48-
60152-49-## directDblClassification
60153-50-
60154-51-The `directDblClassification` method identifies doublets by training a classifier directly on gene expression.
60155:52:This follows the same procedure as `scDblFinder` for doublet generation and iterative training, but skips the _k_-nearest neighbor step and directly uses the matrix of real cells and artificial doublets.
60156:53:This is computationally more intensive and generally leads to worse predictions than `scDblFinder`, and it is included chiefly for comparative purposes.
60157-54-See `?directDblClassification` for more information.
60158-55-
60159-56-## findDoubletClusters
60160-57-
60161-58-The `findDoubletClusters` method identifies clusters that are likely to be composed of doublets by estimating whether their expression profile lies between two other clusters. See [findDoubletClusters](findDoubletClusters.html) for more information.
60162-59-
60163-60-<br/>
60164-61-

60179:76:While the different methods included here have their values, overall the `scDblFinder` method had the best performance (also superior to other methods not included in this package), and should be used by default.

61935-21-
61936:22:# scDblFinder
61937-23-
61938:24:The `scDblFinder` method combines the strengths of various doublet detection approaches, 
61939-25-training an iterative classifier on the neighborhood of real cells and artificial doublets.
61940-26-
61941:27:`scDblFinder()` has two main modes of operation: cluster-based or not.
61942-28-Both perform quite well (see [Germain et al., 2021](https://f1000research.com/articles/10-979)).
61943-29-In general, we recommend the cluster-based approach in datasets with a very clear cluster structure, and the random approach in more complex datasets.
61944-30-
61945-31-## Installation
61946-32-
61947-33-```{r, eval=FALSE}
61948-34-if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
61949-35-    install.packages("BiocManager")
61950:36:BiocManager::install("scDblFinder")
61951-37-
61952-38-# or, to get that latest developments:
61953:39:BiocManager::install("plger/scDblFinder")
61954-40-```
61955-41-
61956-42-## Usage
61957-43-
61958:44:The input of `scDblFinder` is an object `sce` of class `r Biocpkg("SingleCellExperiment")` (empty drops having already been removed) containing at least the counts (assay 'counts'). Alternatively, a simple count matrix can also be provided.
61959-45-
61960:46:Given an SCE object, `scDblFinder` (using the random approach) can be launched as follows :
61961-47-
61962-48-```{r, warning=FALSE}
61963-49-set.seed(123)
61964:50:suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(scDblFinder))
61965-51-# we create a dummy dataset; since it's small we set a higher doublet rate
61966-52-sce <- mockDoubletSCE(dbl.rate=0.1, ngenes=300 )
61967:53:# we run scDblFinder (providing the unusually high doublet rate)
61968:54:sce <- scDblFinder(sce, dbr=0.1)
61969-55-```
61970-56-
61971-57-For 10x data, it is usually safe to leave the `dbr` empty, and it will be automatically estimated.
61972-58-(If using a chip other than the standard 10X, you might have to adjust it or the related `dbr.per1k` argument.
61973-59-
61974:60:`scDblFinder` will add a number of columns to the colData of `sce` prefixed with 'scDblFinder', the most important of which are:
61975-61-
61976:62:* `sce$scDblFinder.score` : the final doublet score
61977:63:* `sce$scDblFinder.class` : the classification (doublet or singlet)
61978-64-
61979-65-We can compare the calls with the truth in this toy example:
61980-66-
61981-67-```{r}
61982:68:table(truth=sce$type, call=sce$scDblFinder.class)
61983-69-```
61984-70-
61985-71-To use the *cluster-based* approach, one simply needs to additionally provide the `clusters` argument:
61986-72-
61987-73-```{r}
61988:74:sce <- scDblFinder(sce, clusters="cluster")
61989:75:table(truth=sce$type, call=sce$scDblFinder.class)
61990-76-```
61991-77-
61992-78-The `clusters` argument can be either a vector of cluster labels for each column of `sce`, a colData column of `sce` containing such labels, or `TRUE`.
61993-79-If `clusters=TRUE`, the fast clustering approach (see `?fastcluster`) will be employed.
61994-80-If normalized expression (assay 'logcounts') and/or PCA (reducedDim 'PCA') are already present in the object, these will be used for the clustering step.
61995-81-
61996-82-### Multiple samples
61997-83-
61998-84-If you have multiple samples (understood as different cell captures), then it is
61999-85-preferable to look for doublets separately for each sample (for multiplexed samples with cell hashes, 
62000-86-this means for each batch). You can do this by simply providing a vector of the sample ids to the 
62001:87:`samples` parameter of `scDblFinder` or, if these are stored in a column of `colData`, the name of the 
62002-88-column. In this case, you might also consider multithreading it using the `BPPARAM` parameter (assuming you've got enough RAM!). 
62003-89-For example:
62004-90-
62005-91-```{r, eval=FALSE}
62006-92-library(BiocParallel)
62007:93:sce <- scDblFinder(sce, samples="sample_id", BPPARAM=MulticoreParam(3))
62008:94:table(sce$scDblFinder.class)
62009-95-```
62010-96-
62011-97-Note that if you are running multiple samples using the cluster-based approach (see below), clustering will be performed sample-wise.
62012:98:While this is typically not an issue for doublet identification, it means that the cluster labels (and putative origins of doublets) won't match between samples. If you are interested in these, it is preferable to first cluster (for example using `sce$cluster <- fastcluster(sce)`) and then provide the clusters to `scDblFinder`, which will ensure concordant labels across samples.
62013-99-
62014-100-Of note, if you have very large differences in number of cells between samples the scores will not be directly comparable. We are working on improving this, but in the meantime it would be preferable to stratify similar samples and threshold the sets separately.
62015-101-
62016-102-<br/><br/>
62017-103-
62018-104-## Description of the method
62019-105-
62020:106:Wrapped in the `scDblFinder` function are the following steps:
62021-107-
62022-108-### Splitting captures
62023-109-
62024:110:Doublets can only arise within a given sample or capture, and for this reason are better sought independently for each sample, which also speeds up the analysis. If the `samples` argument is given, `scDblFinder` will use it to split the cells into samples/captures, and process each of them in parallel if the `BPPARAM` argument is given. Depending on the `multiSampleMode` argument, the classifier can be trained globally, with thresholds optimized on a per-sample basis; however we did not see an improvement in doing so, and therefore by default each sample is treated separately to maximize robustness to technical differences.
62025-111-
62026-112-If your samples are multiplexed, i.e. the different samples are mixed in different batches, then the batches should be what you provide to this argument.
62027-113-
62028-114-### Reducing and clustering the data
62029-115-
62030-116-The analysis can be considerably sped up, at little if any cost in accuracy, by reducing the dataset to only the top expressed genes (controlled by the `nfeatures` argument).
62031-117-
62032-118-Then, depending on the `clusters` argument, an eventual PCA and clustering (using the internal `fastcluster` function) will be performed.
62033---
62034-120-An alternative approach, however, is to generate doublets randomly (setting `clusters` to FALSE or NULL), and use the iterative approach (see below) to exclude also unidentifiable artificial doublets from the training.
62035-121-
62036-122-### Generating artificial doublets
62037-123-
62038-124-Depending on the `clusters` and `propRandom` arguments, artificial doublets will be generated by combining random cells and/or pairs of non-identical clusters (this can be performed manually using the `getArtificialDoublets` function). A proportion of the doublets will simply use the sum of counts of the composing cells, while the rest will undergo a library size adjustment and poisson resampling.
62039-125-
62040-126-### Examining the k-nearest neighbors (kNN) of each cell
62041-127-
62042:128:A new PCA is performed on the combination of real and artificial cells, from which a kNN network is generated. Using this kNN, a number of parameters are gathered for each cell, such as the proportion of doublets (i.e. artificial doublets or known doublets provided through the `knownDoublets` argument, if given) among the KNN, ratio of the distances to the nearest doublet and nearest non-doublet, etc. Several of this features are reported in the output with the 'scDblFinder.' prefix, e.g.:
62043-129-
62044-130-* `distanceToNearest` : distance to the nearest cell (real or artificial)
62045-131-* `ratio` : the proportion of the KNN that are doublets. (If more than one value of `k` is given, the various ratios will be used during classification and will be reported)
62046-132-* `weighted` : the proportion of the KNN that are doublets, weighted by their distance (useful for isolated cells)
62047-133-
62048-134-### Training a classifier
62049-135-
62050:136:Unless the `score` argument is set to 'weighted' or 'ratio' (in which case the aforementioned ratio is directly used as a doublet score), `scDblFinder` then uses gradient boosted trees trained on the kNN-derived properties along with a few additional features (e.g. library size, number of non-zero features, and an estimate of the difficultly of detecting artificial doublets in the cell's neighborhood, a variant of the `cxds` score from the `r Biocpkg("scds","scds")`, etc.) to distinguish doublets (either artificial or given) from other cells, and assigns a score on this basis. 
62051-137-
62052-138-One problem of using a classifier for this task is that some of the real cells (the actual doublets) are mislabeled as singlet, so to speak. 
62053:139:`scDblFinder` therefore iteratively retrains the classifier, each time excluding from the training the (real) cells called as doublets in the previous step (as well as unidentifiable artificial doublets). The number of steps being controlled by the `iter` parameter (in our experience, 2 or 3 is optimal).
62054-140-
62055:141:This score is available in the output, in the `scDblFinder.score` colData column, and can be interpreted as a probability. If the data is multi-sample, a single model is trained for all samples.
62056-142-
62057-143-### Thresholding
62058-144-
62059:145:Rather than thresholding on some arbitrary cutoff of the score, `scDblFinder` uses the expected number of doublets in combination to the misclassification rate to establish a threshold. Unless it is manually given through the `dbr` argument, the expected doublet rate is first estimated (see below). If samples were specified, and if the `dbr` is automatically calculated, thresholding is performed separately across samples.
62060-146-
62061-147-Thresholding then tries to simultaneously minimize: 1) the classification error (in terms of the proportion of known doublets below the threshold) and 2) the deviation from the expected number of doublets among real cells (as a ratio of the total number of expected doublets within the range determined by `dbr.sd`, and adjusted for homotypic doublets). This means that, if you have no idea about the doublet rate, setting `dbr.sd=1` will make the threshold depend entirely on the misclassification rate.
62062-148-
62063-149-### Doublet origins and enrichments
62064-150-
62065-151-If artificial doublets are generated between clusters, it is sometimes possible to call the most likely origin (in terms of the combination of clusters) of a given putative real doublet.
62066-152-We observed that at least one of the two composing cell is typically recognized, but that both are seldom correctly recognized, owing to the sometimes small relative contribution of one of the two original cells.
62067:153:This information is provided through the `scDblFinder.mostLikelyOrigin` column of the output (and the `scDblFinder.originAmbiguous` column indicates whether this origin is ambiguous or rather clear).
62068-154-This, in turn, allows us to identify enrichment over expectation for specific kinds of doublets.
62069:155:Some statistics on each combination of clusters are saved in `metadata(sce)$scDblFinder.stats`, and the `plotDoubletMap` function can be used to visualize enrichments.
62070-156-In addition, two frameworks are offered for testing the significance of enrichments:
62071-157-
62072-158-* The `clusterStickiness` function tests whether each cluster forms more doublet than would be expected given its abundance, by default using a single quasi-binomial model fitted across all doublet types.
62073-159-* The `doubletPairwiseEnrichment` function separately tests whether each specific doublet type (i.e. combination of clusters) is more abundant than expected, by default using a poisson model.
62074-160-
62075-161-<br/><br/>
62076-162-
62077-163-## Some important parameters
62078-164-
62079:165:`scDblFinder` has a fair number of parameters governing the preprocessing, generation of doublets, classification, etc. (see `?scDblFinder`). Here we describe just a few of the most important ones.
62080-166-
62081-167-### Expected proportion of doublets
62082-168-
62083-169-The expected proportion of doublets has no impact on the density of artificial doublets in the neighborhood, but impacts the classifier's score and, especially, where the cutoff will be placed. It is specified through the `dbr` parameter, as well as `dbr.per1k` (which specifies, if `dbr` is omitted, the rate per thousands cells from which to estimate it). In addition, the `dbr.sd` parameter specifies a +/- range around `dbr` within which the deviation from `dbr` will be considered null.
62084-170-
62085-171-For most platforms, the more cells you capture the higher the chance of creating a doublet.
62086-172-For standard 10X data, the 10X documentation indicates a doublet rate of roughly 0.8\% per 1000 cells captured, which is the default value of `dbr.per1k`. This means that unless `dbr` is manually set, with 5000 cells, (0.008\*5)\*5000 = 200 doublets are expected, and the default expected doublet rate will be set to this value (with a default standard deviation of 0.015). Note however that different protocols may vary in the expected proportion of doublets. For example, the high-throughput (HT) 10X kit has an expected doublet rate of half the standard, i.e. 0.4\% per 1000 cells, so if using that kit, set `dbr.per1k=0.004`.
62087-173-
62088-174-Also note that strictly speaking, the proportion of doublets depends more on the number of cells inputted than that recovered. If your recovery rate was lower than expected, you might observe a higher doublet rate (see the [too-many doublets](#toomany) section below).
62089-175-
62090-176-The impact of the expected doublet rate on the thresholding will depend on how hard the classification task is: if it is easy, the called doublets will not depend much on the expected rate. **If you are unsure about the doublet rate, you might consider increasing `dbr.sd`**: with a high value (e.g. 1), the thresholding will be entirely based on the misclassification error (without any assumption about an expected doublet rate).
62091-177-
62092-178-### Number of artificial doublets
62093-179-
62094:180:The number of artificial doublets can be set through the `artificialDoublets` parameter. Using more artificial doublets leads to a better sampling of the possible mixtures of cells, but increases memory and runtime, and can skew the scores, in extreme cases leading to difficulties in setting a threshold for being called as a doublet (see [this issue](https://github.com/plger/scDblFinder/issues/79) for a discussion).
62095-181-
62096:182:By default, `scDblFinder` will generate roughly as many artificial doublets as there are cells, which is usually appropriate. However, for very small datasets this could represent an undersampling of the mixing space and hence lead to lower detection accuracy. For this reason, a hard minimum number of artificial doublet is set. This will tend to improve accuracy for small datasets, but the scores will be skewed towards 1, possibly making a separation difficult. If you are in such a situation and your histogram of scores does not show a bimodality, consider manually setting the `artificialDoublets` parameter to something closer to your actual number of cells.
62097-183-
62098-184-<br/><br/>
62099-185-
62100-186-## Frequently-asked questions
62101-187-
62102-188-### I'm getting way too many doublets called - what's going on? {#toomany}
62103-189-
62104-190-Then you most likely have a wrong doublet rate. If you did not provide it (`dbr` argument), the doublet rate will be calculated automatically using expected doublet rates from 10x, meaning that the more cells captured, the higher the doublet rates. If you have reasons to think that this is not applicable to your data, set the `dbr` manually.
62105-191-
62106:192:The most common cause for an unexpectedly large proportion of doublets is if you have a multi-sample dataset and did not split by samples. `scDblFinder` will think that the data is a single capture with loads of cells, and hence with a very high doublet rate. Splitting by sample should solve the issue.
62107-193-
62108:194:Also note that, although 10X-like data tends to have roughly 1\% per 1000 cells captured, the determining factor for doublet formation is the number of cells inserted into the machine. If for some reason your recovery rate is lower than expected, you might have a higher doublet rate than you'd expect from the captured and called cells (in other words, it would be preferable to say that the doublet rate is roughly 0.6\% per 1000 cells put into the machine, where 0.6 is the recovery rate). In such circumstances, `scDblFinder` typically sets the thresholds correctly nevertheless. This is because the thresholding tries to minimize both the deviation from the expected number of doublets and the misclassification (i.e. of artificial doublets), meaning that the effective (i.e. final) doublet rate will differ from the given one. `scDblFinder` also considers false positives to be less problematic than false negatives. You can reduce to some degree the deviation from the input doublet rate by setting `dbr.sd=0`.
62109-195-
62110-196-Finally, note that version (1.20.0) initially shipped with the current Bioconductor release (3.20) version included a wrong default doublet rate (`dbr.per1k`) argument (it was 0.08 instead of 0.008). This was subsequently fixed in version 1.20.2, but if you installed before that you might need to update the package.
62111-197-
62112-198-### Should I use the cluster-based doublet generation or not?
62113-199-
62114:200:Both approaches perform very similarly overall in benchmarks (see the [scDblFinder paper](https://f1000research.com/articles/10-979/)).
62115-201-If your data is very clearly segregated into clusters, or if you are interested in the origin of the doublets, the cluster-based approach is preferable. This will also enable a more accurate accounting of homotypic doublets, and therefore a slightly better thresholding.
62116-202-Otherwise, and especially if your data does not segregate very clearly into clusters, the random approach (e.g. `clusters=FALSE`, the default) is preferable.
62117-203-
62118-204-### The clusters don't make any sense!
62119-205-
62120:206:If you ran `scDblFinder` on a multi-sample dataset and did not provide the cluster labels, then the labels are sample-specific (meaning that label '1' in one sample might have nothing to do with label '1' in another), and plotting them on a tSNE will look like they do not make sense. For this reason, when running multiple samples we recommend to first cluster all samples together (for example using `sce$cluster <- fastcluster(sce)`) and then provide the clusters to `scDblFinder`.
62121-207-
62122-208-### 'Size factors should be positive' error
62123-209-
62124-210-You will get this error if you have some cells that have zero reads (or a very low read count, leading to zero after feature selection). After filtering out these cells the error should go away.
62125-211-
62126-212-### Identifying homotypic doublets
62127-213-
62128:214:Like other similar tools, scDblFinder focuses on identifying heterotypic doublets (formed by different cell types), and has only a low performance in identifying homotypic doublets (see [this preprint](https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.08.04.552078)). This can lead to disagreements with doublets called using cell hashes or SNPs in multiplexed samples, which capture both types of doublets similarly (and can miss intra-sample heterotypic doublets, especially if the multiplexing is low). This is why we treat these approaches as complementary.
62129-215-
62130:216:However, should you for some reason try to identify also homotypic doublets with scDblFinder, be sure to not to use the cluster-based approach, and to set `removeUnidentifiable=FALSE`. Otherwise, scDblFinder removes artificial doublets likely to be homotypic from training, therefore focusing the task on heterotypic doublets, but at the expense ot homotypic ones (which are typically deemed relatively harmless).
62131-217-
62132-218-### What is a sample exactly? Usage with barcoded and 10X Flex data.
62133-219-
62134-220-As indicated above, the `samples` argument should be used to indicate different captures.
62135-221-For multiplexed samples, this is expected to be the batch of cells processed together, rather than the actual samples.
62136-222-
62137-223-In highly multiplexed datasets such as produced by the 10X Flex kit (especially 16-plex), this can cause two kinds of problems.
62138-224-First, the whole logic of the Flex approach is that inter-sample doublets can be resolved into separate cells, and while a large number of unresolvable intra-sample doublets will remain (see [Howitt et al., 2024](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.03.616596v2)), the expected remaining doublet rate will not be the same as for classical 10X experiment. For this reason, we recommend to set a higher `dbr.sd` in such circumstances, e.g. `dbr.sd=1` to base the thresholding entirely on the classification accuracy.
62139-225-
62140:226:Another, more practical problem is that, with such kits, the very large number of cells in a single capture might translante into very large computational demands when running `scDblFinder`. To circumvent such problem, one can split a batch of cells into more decently-sized chunks and process the chunks separately, so long as each chunk is representative of the whole batch in terms of cell heterogeneity.
62141-227-
62142-228-### How can I make this reproducible?
62143-229-
62144:230:Because it relies on the partly random generation of artificial doublets, running scDblFinder multiple times on the same data will yield slightly different results.
62145-231-You can ensure reproducibility using `set.seed()`, however this will not be sufficient when processing multiple samples (i.e. using the `samples` argument -- even without multithreading!).
62146-232-In such case, the seed needs to be passed to the BPPARAMs:
62147-233-
62148-234-```
62149-235-bp <- MulticoreParam(3, RNGseed=1234)
62150:236:sce <- scDblFinder(sce, clusters="cluster", samples="sample", BPPARAM=bp)
62151-237-```
62152-238-
62153-239-Similarly, when processing the samples serially, use `SerialParam(RNGseed = seed)`.
62154-240-
62155:241:(Note that in `BiocParallel` versions <1.28, one had in addition to explicitly start the cluster before the run using `bpstart(bp)`, and then `bpstop(bp)` after `scDblFinder`.)
62156-242-
62157:243:As a final note: when running `scDblFinder` twice on the same data with different random seeds, the scores will be highly correlated, but some cells will be called as doublets (with a high score) in only one of the runs (e.g. see [this issue](https://github.com/plger/scDblFinder/issues/106)). There are good reasons to believe that these are `homotypic doublets` (if doublets at all), and if you worry chiefly about hetertypic doublets, you may concentrate on those that are reprocibly called across runs.
62158-244-
62159-245-### Can I use this in combination with Seurat or other tools?
62160-246-
62161:247:If the input SCE already contains a `logcounts` assay or a `reducedDim` slot named 'PCA', scDblFinder will use them for the clustering step. In addition, a clustering can be manually given using the `clusters` argument of `scDblFinder()`. In this way, `r Githubpkg("satijalab.org/seurat")` clustering could for instance be used to create the artificial doublets (see `?Seurat::as.SingleCellExperiment.Seurat` for conversion to SCE).
62162-248-For example, assuming as `Seurat` object `se`, the following could be done:
62163-249-
62164-250-```

62166-252-# port the resulting scores back to the Seurat object:
62167:253:se$scDblFinder.score <- sce$scDblFinder.score
62168-254-```
62169-255-

62171:257:If you wish this step to be performed differently, you may provide your own function for doing so (see the ``processing`` argument in `?scDblFinder`). We note, however, that the impact of variations of this step on doublet detection is rather mild.
62172-258-In fact, not performing any normalization at all for instance decreases doublet identification accuracy, but by rather little.
62173-259-

62223-309-

62225-311-
62226-312-### Should I run QC cell filtering before or after doublet detection?
62227-313-
62228:314:The input to `scDblFinder` should not include empty droplets, and it might be necessary to remove cells with a very low coverage (e.g. <200 or 500 reads) to avoid errors.
62229-315-Further quality filtering should be performed _downstream_ of doublet detection, for two reasons:
62230:316:1. the default expected doublet rate is calculated on the basis of the cells given, and if you excluded a lot of cells as low quality, `scDblFinder` might think that the doublet rate should be lower than it is.
62231-317-2. kicking out all low quality cells first might hamper our ability to detect doublets that are formed by the combination of a good quality cell with a low-quality one.
62232-318-This being said, these are mostly theoretical grounds, and unless your QC filtering is very stringent (and it shouldn't be!), it's unlikely to make a big difference.
62233-319-
62234-320-#### What about ambiant RNA decontamination?
62235-321-
62236-322-Contamination by ambiant RNA has emerged as an important confounder in single-cell (and especially single-nuclei) RNAseq data, which prompts the question of whether that should be run prior or after doublet detection. 
62237-323-Unfortunately, we do not currently have good evidence pointing in either direction, and arguments can be made for both.
62238-324-Low-quality doublets, or doublets from an experiment with a large dominant celltype, can easily look like contamination, and likewise a high amount of contamination can easily look like a doublet because it includes RNA from other cell types.
62239-325-There is a possibility that a decontamination package sees an actual doublet as contamination, and attempts to clean it, which it will necessarily do imperfectly (because while the decontamination is a mixture of all cells, a doublet isn't), but perhaps sufficiently so that it can't be accurately detected as a doublet anymore. This would therefore be an argument for running doublet calling first. 
62240-326-However, it's also possible that decontamination, because it makes the cells cleaner, makes the doublet detection task easier.
62241-327-
62242-328-### Can I combine this method with others?
62243-329-
62244-330-Of course it is always possible to run multiple methods and combine the results.
62245:331:In our benchmark, the combination of scDblFinder with DoubletFinder, for instance, did yield an improvement in most (though not all) datasets (see [the results here](https://github.com/plger/scDblFinder/issues/67#issuecomment-1353590091)), although of a small magnitude.
62246-332-The simplest way is to do an average of the scores (assuming that the scores are on a similar scale, and that a higher score has the same interpretation across methods), which for instance gave similar results to using a Fisher p-value combination on 1-score (interpreted as a probability).

62321-22-# Introduction
62322-23-
62323-24-Analyses in single-cell RNAseq are typically limited to a relatively small (e.g. one or two thousands) set of features that are most informative; these are often the genes with a higher expression (and hence more chances of being quantified).
62324-25-In contrast, single-cell ATACseq (scATACseq) data is considerably more sparse, with most reads being spread across hundreds of thousands of regions.
62325-26-In this context, selecting a subset of genes is highly ineffective, and therefore many of the methods developed for single-cell RNAseq are not easily applicable, and need to be adapted.
62326-27-Methods have therefore been developed specifically for scATACseq data (Granja et al. 2021; Thibodeau et al. 2021).
62327-28-
62328:29:This vignette presents different approaches to doublet detection in single-cell ATAC-seq implemented in the package: the first is an adaptation of `scDblFinder`, the second a reimplementation of the AMULET method from Thibodeau et al. (2021). The latter has the advantage of capturing homotypic doublets, but does not perform well in all datasets, and especially requires the cells to have a high library size. We therefore next present two ways of combining the two.
62329-30-
62330:31:# Applying the scDblFinder method
62331-32-
62332:33:With default parameters, the `scDblFinder` method performs very poorly on scATACseq data due to the increase spread of the reads across many features. Since working with all features (i.e. tiles or peaks) is computationally very expensive, an alternative approach is to begin by reducing the size of the dataset, not through _selection_ (as in scRNAseq), but by _aggregating_ correlated features into a relatively small set.
62333-34-This has the advantage of using all information, as well as making the count data more continuous.
62334-35-This method yields comparable performance to specialized single-cell ATACseq software (Germain et al., 2021).
62335-36-
62336-37-The feature aggregation can be triggered using the `aggregateFeatures=TRUE` argument, which will aggregate peak or tile counts into the number of meta-features defined by the `nfeatures`.
62337-38-If the number of meta-features is low (which we recommend), the meta-features can be directly used to calculated distances rather than going through the SVD step (which can be triggered with the `processing` argument). Such an example would be:
62338-39-
62339-40-```{r}
62340:41:suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(scDblFinder))
62341-42-# we use a dummy SingleCellExperiment as example:
62342-43-sce <- mockDoubletSCE(ngenes=300)
62343-44-# setting low number of artificial doublets (same as ncells) just for speedup:
62344:45:sce <- scDblFinder(sce, artificialDoublets=1, aggregateFeatures=TRUE, nfeatures=25, processing="normFeatures")
62345-46-```
62346-47-
62347-48-If you encounter problems running the aggregation-based approach on large datasets, first make sure you have the `mbkmeans` package installed.
62348-49-
62349-50-# Using the Amulet method
62350-51-
62351:52:The AMULET method from Thibodeau et al. (2021) is based on the assumption that, in a diploid cell, any given genomic region should be captured at most twice. Therefore, cells with loci covered by more than two fragments are indicative of the droplet being a doublet. Of note, this approach has the advantage of capturing homotypic doublets, which instead tend to be missed by other methods. Since it was only available in the form of a mixture of java and python scripts, we re-implemented the method in `scDblFinder` (see `?amulet`), leading to equal or superior results to the original implementation (Germain et al. 2021).
62352-53-
62353-54-As in the original implementation, we recommend excluding the mitochondrial and sex chromosomes, as well as repetitive regions. This can be specified with the `regionsToExclude` argument (see the underlying `?getFragmentOverlaps`). It can be used as follows:
62354-55-
62355-56-```{r}
62356-57-# here we use a dummy fragment file for example:

62358-59-
62359-60-# we might also give a GRanges of repeat elements, so that these regions are excluded:
62360-61-suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(GenomicRanges))
62361-62-repeats <- GRanges("chr6", IRanges(1000,2000))
62362-63-# it's better to combine these with mitochondrial and sex chromosomes
62363-64-otherChroms <- GRanges(c("M","chrM","MT","X","Y","chrX","chrY"),IRanges(1L,width=10^8))
62364-65-# here since I don't know what chromosome notation you'll be using I've just put them all,
62365-66-# although this will trigger a warning when combining them:
62366-67-toExclude <- suppressWarnings(c(repeats, otherChroms))
62367-68-# we then launch the method
62368-69-res <- amulet(fragfile, regionsToExclude=toExclude)
62369-70-res
62370-71-```
62371-72-
62372:73:The results is a data.frame with statistics for each barcode, including a p-value. In contrast to the `scDblFinder` score, a lower p-value here is indicative of the droplet being more likely to be a doublet (as in the original method).
62373-74-By default, only the barcodes with a minimum number of reads are considered, but it is possible to specify the droplets for which to gather statistics using the `barcodes` argument.
62374-75-
62375-76-While the package includes an implementation that works based on peak/tile count matrices (see `?amuletFromCounts`), it has a much lower performance with respect to the one based directly on the fragment files (see `?amulet`), and we therefore discourage its use.
62376-77-
62377-78-The workhorse behind the `amulet` function is the `getFragmentOverlaps`, which also includes all of the relevant arguments.
62378-79-If the fragment files are not Tabix-indexed, the whole fragment file will have to be loaded in memory for processing; while this ensures relatively rapid computation, it has high memory requirements. Therefore, if the fragment file is Tabix-indexed (as is for instance done as part of the ArchR pipeline), it will be read and processed per chromosome, which is a little slower due to overhead, but keeps memory requirements rather low. This behavior can be disabled by specifying `fullInMemory=TRUE`.
62379-80-
62380-81-# Combining mehtods
62381-82-
62382:83:While the `scDblFinder`-based approach generally performs well, none of the two approach is optimal across all datasets tested. We therefore investigated two strategies for combining the rationales of each approach.
62383-84-
62384:85:The Amulet method tends to perform best with datasets that have homotypic doublets and where cells have a high library size (i.e. median library size per cell of 10-15k reads), while the `scDblFinder`-based approach works better for heterotypic doublets. Until an optimal solution is found, we recommend using multiple approaches to inform decisions, in particular using the p-value combination method below.
62385-86-
62386-87-## The Clamulet method
62387-88-
62388:89:The `clamulet` method (Classification-powered Amulet-like method) operates similarly to the `scDblFinder` method, but generates artificial doublets by operating on the fragment coverages. This has the advantage that the number of loci covered by more than two reads can be computed for artificial doublets, enabling the use of this feature (along with the kNN-based ones) in a classification scheme. It however has the disadvantage of being rather slow and memory hungry, and appears to be outperformed by a simple p-value combination of the two methods (see below). We therefore _do not_ recommend its usage.
62389-90-
62390:91:The `clamulet` method uses the aforementioned aggregation approach, and its usage includes a number of arguments from both the `scDblFinder` and `amulet` method (see in particular `?getFragmentOverlaps`):
62391-92-
62392-93-```{r, eval=FALSE}
62393-94-# not run
62394-95-d <- clamulet("path/to/fragments.tsv.gz")
62395-96-```
62396-97-
62397-98-Since our dummy fragment file is so small (5 barcodes), here we'll have to adjust the arguments for an example to run:
62398-99-
62399-100-```{r}
62400-101-d <- clamulet(fragfile, k=2, nfeatures=3)
62401-102-d
62402-103-```
62403-104-
62404:105:The score can then be interpreted as for `scDblFinder`. We however note that this method proved *inferior to alternatives*.
62405-106-
62406-107-## Simple p-value combination
62407-108-
62408:109:The amulet and scDblFinder scores above can be simply combined by treating them as p-values and aggregating them (here using Fisher's method from the `r CRANpkg("aggregation")` package, but see also the `r CRANpkg("metap")` package):
62409-110-

62513-23-
62514-24-# Introduction
62515-25-
62516:26:The `scDblFinder` package gathers various methods for the detection and handling of doublets/multiplets in single-cell sequencing data (i.e. multiple cells captured within the same droplet or reaction volume).
62517-27-This vignette provides a brief overview of the different approaches (which are each covered in their own vignettes) for single-cell RNA sequencing. 
62518-28-*For doublet detection in genomic data, see the [scATACseq vignette](scATAC.html)*. 
62519-29-For a more general introduction to the topic of doublets, refer to the [OCSA book](https://osca.bioconductor.org/doublet-detection.html).
62520-30-
62521-31-All methods require as an input either a matrix of counts or a `r Biocpkg("SingleCellExperiment")` containing count data. With the exception of [findDoubletClusters](findDoubletClusters.html), which operates at the level of clusters (and consequently requires clustering information), all methods try to assign each cell a score indicating its likelihood (broadly understood) of being a doublet.
62522-32-
62523-33-The approaches described here are _complementary_ to doublets identified via cell hashes and SNPs in multiplexed samples: while hashing/genotypes can identify doublets formed by cells of the same type (homotypic doublets) from two samples, which are often nearly undistinguishable from real cells transcriptionally (and hence generally unidentifiable through the present package), it cannot identify doublets made by cells of the same sample, even if they are heterotypic (formed by different cell types). Indeed, recent evidence suggests that doublets are for instance a serious and strongly underestimated issue in 10x Flex datasets (see [Howitt et al., 2024](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.10.03.616596v2)). Instead, the methods presented here are primarily geared towards the identification of heterotypic doublets, which for most purposes are also the most critical ones.
62524-34-
62525---
62526-37-## computeDoubletDensity
62527-38-
62528-39-The `computeDoubletDensity` method (formerly `scran::doubletCells`) generates random artificial doublets from the real cells, and tries to identify cells whose neighborhood has a high local density of articial doublets. See [computeDoubletDensity](computeDoubletDensity.html) for more information.
62529-40-
62530-41-## recoverDoublets
62531-42-
62532-43-The `recoverDoublets` method is meant to be used when some doublets are already known, for instance through genotype-based calls or cell hashing in multiplexed experiments. The function then tries to identify intra-sample doublets that are neighbors to the known inter-sample doublets. See [recoverDoublets](recoverDoublets.html) for more information.
62533-44-
62534:45:## scDblFinder
62535-46-
62536:47:The `scDblFinder` method combines both known doublets (if available) and cluster-based artificial doublets to identify doublets. The approach builds and improves on a variety of earlier efforts, and is at present the most accurate approach included in this package. See [scDblFinder](scDblFinder.html) for more information.
62537-48-
62538-49-## directDblClassification
62539-50-
62540-51-The `directDblClassification` method identifies doublets by training a classifier directly on gene expression.
62541:52:This follows the same procedure as `scDblFinder` for doublet generation and iterative training, but skips the _k_-nearest neighbor step and directly uses the matrix of real cells and artificial doublets.
62542:53:This is computationally more intensive and generally leads to worse predictions than `scDblFinder`, and it is included chiefly for comparative purposes.
62543-54-See `?directDblClassification` for more information.
62544-55-
62545-56-## findDoubletClusters
62546-57-
62547-58-The `findDoubletClusters` method identifies clusters that are likely to be composed of doublets by estimating whether their expression profile lies between two other clusters. See [findDoubletClusters](findDoubletClusters.html) for more information.
62548-59-
62549-60-<br/>
62550-61-

62562-73-# Which method to choose?
62563-74-
62564:75:A benchmark of the main methods available in the package is presented in the [scDblFinder paper](https://f1000research.com/articles/10-979/).
62565:76:While the different methods included here have their values, overall the `scDblFinder` method had the best performance (also superior to other methods not included in this package), and should be used by default.

62575-2-title: Recovering intra-sample doublets 
62576:3:package: scDblFinder
62577-4-author: 
62578-5-- name: Aaron Lun

62586-68-
62587-69-The most problematic assumption is that required to obtain $N_{intra}$ from $\vec S$.
62588-70-Obtaining a better estimate would require, at least, the knowledge of the two parent states for each doublet population.
62589-71-This can be determined with some simulation-based heuristics but it is likely to be more trouble than it is worth.
62590-72-
62591-73-In this theoretical framework, we can easily spot a case where our method fails.
62592-74-If both $C_1$ and $C_2$ are unique to a given sample, all events in $D_{12}$ will be intra-sample doublets.
62593-75-This means that no events in $D_{12}$ will ever be detected as inter-sample doublets, which precludes their detection as intra-sample doublets by `recoverDoublets`.
62594:76:The computational remedy is to augment the predictions with simulation-based methods (e.g., `scDblFinder()`) while the experimental remedy is to ensure that multiplexed samples include technical or biological replicates.
